sections.text: Last lesson we wrote pure functions that turn request text into response text. Now we connect them to the network. The standard library has everything needed: TcpListener waits for connections, and TcpStream is one open connection that you can read from and write to.

A server starts like this: TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0"). 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address, which only reaches your own computer, and it is the only kind of address the sandbox in this app allows. The 0 after the colon means "pick any free port for me". local_addr() tells you which one was chosen. Then listener.accept() waits for one client to connect, and listener.incoming() gives you each new connection in turn.

The code uses some parts of std::io that are new. A stream carries bytes, so as_bytes() turns text into bytes before it is sent. Methods like read_to_string, write_all and read_line come from traits (Read, Write and BufRead), and a trait's methods only work when you import it with use, as in Unit 7. The write! and writeln! macros work like print! and println!, but send the text into a stream instead of the screen. BufReader::new(&stream) wraps a stream so you can read it one line at a time. read_line adds one line, including its \r\n, to a String and returns how many bytes it read; 0 means the other side has closed the connection. A SocketAddr is a value that holds an IP address and a port.

Our program does the whole conversation in one process, so you can see both sides. A server thread accepts exactly three connections and starts a new thread for each one. Three client threads connect, send a GET request and read the answer. Reading with read_to_string finishes when the server closes the connection, which happens when the server's TcpStream is dropped at the end of handle. We join the clients in the order we started them, so the output is always the same.

Because every connection gets its own thread, a slow client cannot block the others. That is the idea behind a simple threaded server. A real server would loop over listener.incoming() forever, instead of stopping after three connections, and would use a thread pool (a fixed set of worker threads) so a flood of clients cannot create unlimited threads. The Rust Book's final chapter builds exactly that.

A port is like an apartment number: the address 127.0.0.1 is the building (your own computer) and the port picks the door. A browser uses port 80 for http:// and 443 for https:// unless the address says otherwise. Using port 0 asks the system for any door that is free, which avoids clashes with other programs.

This is the thread-per-connection model, the same as a classic blocking Java or C server. It is simple and handles hundreds of clients well; for tens of thousands of mostly idle connections, async code (previous unit) with tokio is the usual choice. For real HTTP you would use hyper, axum or actix-web, which handle keep-alive, chunked bodies, TLS and more. Note that the Connection: close header only tells a real client not to wait for more; closing the stream (the drop at the end of handle) is what ends our client's read_to_string.

exercise.prompt: This echo server sends the client's line straight back. Change it so the server shouts: it should reply with the same line in upper case. The program should print: HELLO. Hint: build the reply with line.trim().to_uppercase().

quiz.question: What does binding to "127.0.0.1:0" do?
options: Listens on every computer connected to the internet at once, on any free port
Uses 0 as a real port number that clients must connect to
Listens only on this computer, on a free port the operating system picks

quiz.question: Why does our client's read_to_string finish?
options: The server closes the connection when its TcpStream is dropped
It gives up after waiting one second for more data to arrive
It stops as soon as the first line of the reply has been received

quiz.question: Why does the server handle each connection in its own thread?
options: Rust requires a separate thread for every TcpStream you create
A slow client then can't block the other clients from being served
Threads make each response shorter, so it travels faster over the connection
